name: What Requirements Are
title: What Requirements Are
description: A requirement is a singular statement of what the system must do or be - one need, one sentence, verifiable. Good requirements are the contract between the asker and the builder.
how_it_works: Write each requirement as one verifiable statement using 'shall' for mandatory and 'should' for desired. If you cannot imagine a test that would prove it, rewrite it until you can.
key_points: One requirement, one need, one verifiable statement.
'Shall' for mandatory, 'should' for desired - use deliberately.
Every requirement must be testable in principle.
Requirements are the contract; everything else is interpretation.
requirements: A stakeholder need statement; defined system boundary; measurable acceptance criteria per requirement.
standards: INCOSE-style requirements practice: each requirement singular, measurable, verifiable; constraints classified by type.
citations: INCOSE Systems Engineering Handbook - requirements definition practices.
IEEE 29148 systems and software engineering - requirements processes.

name: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
description: Functional requirements say what the system does (dispense 500 ml); non-functional requirements say how well (within 5 seconds, under 60 dB). Both are mandatory; non-functional ones are the most often forgotten.
how_it_works: List functions first, then attach quality attributes to each: performance, reliability, usability, safety, environmental. Give every non-functional requirement a number - 'fast' is not a requirement, 'under 5 seconds' is.
key_points: Functional: what it does. Non-functional: how well.
Non-functional requirements need numbers, not adjectives.
Attach quality attributes to each function.
Forgotten non-functionals become expensive surprises.

name: Constraints: The Limits That Shape Design
title: Constraints: The Limits That Shape Design
description: Constraints are the non-negotiable limits: budget caps, size envelopes, regulatory rules, available tools, deadlines. They shape the design space more than requirements do.
how_it_works: Collect constraints early and classify them (cost, size, regulatory, resource, time). Treat each as a hard boundary in every design decision - a design that violates a constraint is not a design, it is a wish.
key_points: Constraints are hard limits: cost, size, regulation, resources, time.
Collect and classify them before designing.
Every design decision is checked against every constraint.
Violating a constraint invalidates the design.

title: Stakeholder Needs Elicitation
description: Requirements come from stakeholders' real needs, found by asking, watching, and reading - not by guessing. Elicitation is detective work: what they say, what they do, and what they assume.

key_points: Needs are found by asking, observing, and reading - not guessing.
Record needs in stakeholder words before translating.
Watch the real work; people cannot fully describe what they do.

name: Writing Testable Requirements
title: Writing Testable Requirements
description: A requirement is only as good as its test. 'The system shall be reliable' is untestable; 'the system shall operate 8,760 hours with no more than 2 failures' is testable - and therefore engineerable.
how_it_works: Attach a verification method to every requirement as you write it (test, inspection, analysis, demonstration) and include the numbers that define pass. If no method fits, the requirement needs rewriting.
key_points: Attach a verification method to each requirement at writing time.
Numbers define pass/fail - adjectives do not.
Untestable requirements are decoration, not engineering.
The test you imagine while writing is the design's first check.
requirements: A stakeholder need statement; defined system boundary; measurable acceptance criteria per requirement.

Owners defend requirements; the list defends itself otherwise.

title: Requirements Traceability Matrices
description: A traceability matrix links requirements forward to design elements and tests, and backward to stakeholder needs. It proves every requirement is addressed and every design element is justified.
how_it_works: Build the matrix as requirements are approved, fill design and test columns as work proceeds, and audit for orphans in both directions. An orphan requirement is unverified; an orphan design element is unjustified.
key_points: Forward: requirement to design to test. Backward: to stakeholder need.
Orphan requirements are unverified; orphan designs are unjustified.
Build the matrix early; audit it at milestones.
The matrix is the proof of completeness.

description: Requirements change - the discipline is in managing change, not preventing it. Every change gets impact analysis (cost, schedule, other requirements) before approval.

key_points: Change is managed, not prevented.
Impact analysis (cost, schedule, ripple) precedes approval.
Update traceability and re-verify affected tests.
Emergencies get retroactive paperwork, never exemption.

Record decisions with rationale for future review.
Trade-off analysis turns arguments into decisions.

key_points: Prioritize explicitly: Must/Should/Could/Won't or weighted scoring.
Priority is a recorded attribute, not a feeling.
Cuts follow priority order by rule.
Everything-equal is the most expensive prioritization.

name: Formal Requirements Reviews

description: Requirements reviews with stakeholders and implementers catch ambiguity, conflict, and untestability before design starts. A reviewed requirement set is a project asset; an unreviewed one is a risk register.
how_it_works: Walk each requirement asking: is it clear, testable, necessary, feasible, and free of design prescription? Record findings as defects against the requirements document and re-review after fixes.
key_points: Review for clarity, testability, necessity, feasibility.
Findings are defects - track and re-review them.
Include implementers: they spot unbuildable requirements.
Reviewed requirements are assets; unreviewed are risks.

name: Constraint-Driven Design Methods
title: Constraint-Driven Design Methods
description: Constraint-driven design treats constraints as the primary design input: the feasible region is mapped first, then optimized within it. It prevents beautiful designs that violate reality.
how_it_works: Map the constraint boundaries quantitatively, search the feasible region for candidate designs, and optimize within it. Document which constraints bind the optimum - they are the next innovation targets.
key_points: Map feasible region first, optimize inside it.
Quantify constraint boundaries, don't just list them.
Binding constraints are the innovation targets.
Feasibility before optimality, always.
requirements: A stakeholder need statement; defined system boundary; measurable acceptance criteria per requirement.

name: Requirements Reuse and Product Lines
title: Requirements Reuse and Product Lines
description: Product families reuse requirement sets with variation points - one managed set serves many products. Reuse without management becomes copy-paste drift; with management it becomes leverage.
how_it_works: Maintain a common requirement core with defined variation points, and derive product-specific sets by resolving variations. Manage the core as its own deliverable with its own reviews.
key_points: Common core plus variation points serves product families.
Derive product sets by resolving variations - not copy-paste.
The core is a managed deliverable with reviews.
Reuse is leverage only when the core is controlled.

description: Requirements quality can be measured: ambiguity counts, testability percentage, volatility, traceability coverage. What gets measured gets improved - including requirements.
how_it_works: Track metrics like percent testable, review defect density, change volatility, and trace coverage. Set quality gates (e.g., 100% testable before design) and hold them.
key_points: Metrics: testability %, defect density, volatility, trace coverage.

name: Agile Requirements: Backlogs Done Right
title: Agile Requirements: Backlogs Done Right
description: Agile backlogs are requirements by another name - and they need the same discipline: clear, testable, prioritized, traced. 'Agile' never meant 'unwritten'.
how_it_works: Write backlog items with acceptance criteria (testable!), prioritize by value, and keep the backlog groomed. Trace items to the needs they serve - velocity without direction is just speed.
key_points: Backlog items need acceptance criteria - testable, always.
Prioritize by value; groom continuously.
Trace items to stakeholder needs.
Agile means adaptive, not undocumented.
